title: Modelling Concept Drift in Dynamic Data Streams for Recommender Systems
authors: Caroprese, L.; Pisani, F.S.; Veloso, B.M.; Konig, M.; Manco, G.; Hoos, H.; Gama, J.
tldr: A stream-based synthetic data generator for recommender systems models concept drift through dynamic tripartite graph embeddings, producing realistic preference data streams with controllable drift dynamics.
problem_and_motivation: The limited availability of large-scale public datasets with realistic temporal properties hampers the development and evaluation of streaming recommendation algorithms. Existing synthetic data generators fail to account for the dynamic nature of user preferences, ignoring concept drift in streaming scenarios. This gap prevents controlled benchmarking of recommendation systems under realistic distributional shifts.
approach: Adopt a matrix factorization framework with Bayesian Personalized Ranking to learn user and item latent embeddings from real data streams.
Represent user-item preferences as a weighted tripartite graph connecting users, latent features, and items.
Use the HDDMW drift detection algorithm to monitor BPR loss and identify regime transitions in the data stream.
Train a sequence of factorization models, one per detected regime, to capture evolving data distributions.
Generate synthetic preference samples from each regime's learned embedding model using Zipf-distributed item frequencies.
Extend the latent space dimensionality by delta K columns when drift is detected, penalizing divergence from the previous model.
Evaluate on three real datasets: Microsoft News (MIND), Amazon Video Games, and Yoochoose.
Compare the adaptive BPR approach against a variational autoencoder baseline across all datasets.
Conduct ablation studies: train on first regime only and train on random sample ignoring stream structure.
findings: The generator produces frequency distributions closely matching the original stream on the MIND dataset, confirmed by positive Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests.
On MIND, the model detected multiple drifts with HR@5 values around 0.6 near drift points but maintained good overall HR@10 performance.
On the original Amazon Video Games dataset, the generator produced significantly worse distributions due to insufficient item preferences.
After inverting users and items in Amazon Video Games (more users than items), synthetic distributions closely matched the original.
num: 7 regimes detected in the Amazon Video Games dataset, indicating 6 drifts.
The VAE baseline outperformed BPR on MIND in stable periods but degraded with new items; BPR adapted faster to distribution shifts.
Ablation study confirmed that training only on the first regime yields good performance only within that regime and fails on subsequent drifts.
A model trained on a random 30% sample across all regimes performed comparably to the streaming approach but is unrealistic for real-world use.
The framework identifies six drift directions: user taste changes, new trends, new users, new items, user churn, and item obsolescence.

num: Three benchmark datasets used: MIND (750K users, 19K items, 3.96M preferences), Amazon Video Games (26K users, 568K items, 825K preferences), Yoochoose (143K users, 10K items, 642K interactions).

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper introduces a novel stream-based synthetic data generator that models concept drift in recommender systems through dynamic tripartite graph embeddings. It provides the first systematic categorization of six drift directions in preference data: user taste changes, emerging trends, new users, new items, user churn, and item obsolescence. The approach learns a sequence of matrix factorization models from real data streams, where each model captures a specific regime's distribution, and transitions between regimes are triggered by drift detection. The work demonstrates that latent embedding modifications can realistically simulate evolving preference streams, enabling controlled benchmarking of streaming recommendation algorithms. A general stream generator framework (Algorithm 2) is provided that maps parameterized drift operations to changes in the underlying graph structure.
directly_justifies: Concept drifts can be modeled as modifications of latent embeddings represented as rewiring changes in the underlying tripartite graph.
The proposed model captures actual preference distributions and generates synthetic streams with similar yet controllable drift dynamics.
The stream-based data generator is the first systematic approach to producing preference data with configurable concept drift in recommender systems.
Adequate item preference counts are essential for the generator to accurately replicate real data distributions.
The adaptive BPR model outperforms a VAE baseline when new items frequently appear in the stream.
limits: The generator's fidelity degrades when the number of preferences per item is insufficient, as shown on the original Amazon Video Games dataset.
The framework relies on the BPR matrix factorization assumption of geometric closeness in latent space for modeling preferences.
The approach cannot generate regimes that deviate from models extracted from the original data stream.
Experiments were limited to three benchmark datasets from different domains; broader validation is needed.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned for citeable claims. Domain 14 (Synthetic Data Generation for Financial ML) was flagged as high relevance since the paper's core contribution is a synthetic data stream generator with concept drift, directly mapping to 14.A. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was flagged as high relevance because the paper proposes a matrix factorization predictive model with BPR optimization, directly addressing 6.A. Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) was flagged as medium relevance for its comprehensive experimental evaluation with HitRate metrics, mapping to 12.B. Domain 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles) was flagged as medium relevance because the paper discusses profile dynamics and cold-start handling for new users/items, mapping to 5.B. Domain 8 (Anomaly Detection) was flagged as low relevance since drift detection algorithms are used but the paper does not focus on anomaly detection in the personal finance sense, mapping to 8.A. Borderline cases included Domain 14.B (ML Model Serving), which was rejected as the paper does not address deployment or serving infrastructure, and Domain 14.C (On-Device vs. Server Inference), which was rejected as no inference architecture discussion is present. Domains 1-4 (Filipino demographics, culturally specific practices, expense categorization, existing PF systems), Domain 7 (Budgeting strategies), Domains 9-11 (Mobile design, data privacy, engagement), and Domain 13 (Savings/debt management) were all rejected as the paper addresses recommender systems generally, not personal finance system design. The overall topical coverage centers on synthetic data generation for streaming recommendation with predictive modeling and evaluation.

limitations: Generator fidelity degrades significantly when the number of preferences per item is insufficient to train an effective model.
The approach relies on the BPR matrix factorization assumption of geometric closeness in latent space, which may not generalize to all preference modeling strategies.
The framework cannot generate regimes that deviate from models extracted from the original data stream, limiting fully independent synthetic generation.
Experiments were limited to three benchmark datasets from different domains; broader validation across more domains is needed.
The VAE baseline comparison could not be executed for the original Amazon Video Games dataset due to excessive memory requirements.
The drift detection performance depends on the choice of loss signal, which may vary across application domains.
remember_this: Synthetic data generator models concept drift through dynamic tripartite graph embeddings in recommender systems.
Generator achieves close distribution matching on MIND dataset but degrades with sparse item preferences.
Adaptive BPR model outperforms VAE when new items frequently appear in the stream.
Six drift directions identified: user taste changes, new trends, new users, new items, user churn, item obsolescence.
Ablation study confirms regime identification is essential for capturing concept drift in streaming data.
